text: Every VM gets one or more virtual CPUs, but a vCPU isn't a dedicated physical core — it's a slice of time on a real core that the hypervisor's scheduler hands out, the same way an operating system schedules processes on a single core. If a host has 8 physical cores running 20 VMs, the hypervisor is constantly switching which vCPU executes where, for a few milliseconds at a time.

That only runs smoothly because of hardware-assisted virtualization. Intel VT-x and AMD-V are CPU extensions built into virtually every modern processor for exactly this job. Before they existed, a hypervisor had to software-emulate privileged CPU instructions, which was slow. VT-x and AMD-V let the hypervisor trap and handle those instructions directly in hardware, which is what makes a modern VM run close to native speed instead of noticeably slower emulation.

Storage works the same way, conceptually: a VM's hard drive isn't a separate physical disk, it's a virtual disk — really just one large file sitting on the host's own filesystem. VMware calls this format VMDK; Microsoft Hyper-V uses VHD or the newer VHDX. From inside the guest OS, that file looks and behaves exactly like a real hard drive with its own drive letter.

Virtual disks can be thick-provisioned, where the full size is reserved on the host disk immediately, or thin-provisioned, where the file only grows as the guest actually writes data. Thin provisioning is the common default when you want to pack more VMs onto limited physical storage — as long as someone keeps an eye on the host disk so it doesn't run out of real space.

Memory works similarly to CPU: the hypervisor maps the guest's view of RAM onto the host's actual physical RAM, using hardware features like Intel EPT or AMD RVI to do that translation efficiently, and can even overcommit memory across VMs that aren't all using their full allocation at once.

CPU scheduling, hardware-assisted virtualization, and virtual disks are the three pieces that actually make a VM function. Next, Lesson 21 compares all of this to a lighter alternative: containers, which skip the full guest OS entirely.
